title: 'No need' to shoot B.C. woman, chief tells RCMP
article: It began as a noisy argument between Lorraine Jacobson and her boyfriend, escalated after two neighbours called 911 to report a domestic dispute and ended with a Mountie fatally shooting Ms. Jacobson in the heart.

Yesterday, as police and aboriginal leaders released details of Ms. Jacobson's shooting last Friday night, natives mourned her death at a memorial service on Cormorant Island, off the northeast coast of Vancouver Island.
Ms. Jacobson, 40, was shot once in the chest and pronounced dead at Alert Bay Hospital. Constable Russ Chanin, who responded to the 911 complaints, is now off duty with pay and receiving counselling.
Still fresh in the minds of mourners yesterday was an emotional meeting on Tuesday night in which natives say they grilled the RCMP, but left after 21⁄2 hours, dissatisfied with the answers.
"Our major message is that there was no need to shoot," said William Cranmer, chief of the Namgis First Nation, which has the main reserve on Cormorant Island.
"Our perception is that the RCMP is doing damage control."
He said anger toward the RCMP lingers, mixed with guilt because two native neighbours called the police after hearing yelling outside Ms. Jacobson's home in the aboriginal community of Whe-La-La-U.
Those two neighbours are upset that their emergency call resulted in Ms. Jacobson's death, Mr. Cranmer said.

He identified Ms. Jacobson's boyfriend as Ernest Joseph, who is believed to be in his late 30s. Mr. Joseph and a friend, Dion Alfred, were drinking alcohol at the Whe-La-La-U duplex, the Namgis chief said.
"The police aren't being very straightforward with their answers," said Michael (Jake) Jacobson, 44, a cousin of Ms. Jacobson's.
RCMP Sergeant Lee Omilusik said the police constable got into Ms. Jacobson's home after someone inside unlocked a sliding glass door, and then the officer saw the woman holding a large butcher knife.
Ms. Jacobson, whose 10-year-old daughter was home at the time, threatened one of the native men inside but then headed toward the constable, Sgt. Omilusik said.
After she refused to drop the knife after three warnings, the police officer fired a single bullet into her, he said.
"Tuesday night's meeting was emotional, but we thought it was productive and helpful," he said. "It's one step in the healing process."
But Mr. Cranmer said natives do not see how the police explanation justifies the fatality.

Other neighbours demanded a fuller account, which Sgt. Omilusik promised will be released after a coroner's inquest and a separate investigation by the RCMP's major crime unit from Courtenay on Vancouver Island.

"This community is still in shock and wondering why it happened. The police are somebody who we're supposed to trust. Now, it's like you can't trust them," said Kelly Scheck, a neighbour who lives a few doors away from Ms. Jacobson's home.
A funeral service will be held on Saturday in North Vancouver.

Lawrence Ambers, band administrator for the Namgis First Nation, whose reserve surrounds Whe-La-La-U, said the argument between Ms. Jacobson and her boyfriend took place outdoors before 8 p.m. last Friday.
Then the couple went indoors, and minutes later, witnesses reported seeing a police officer attempting to kick in the front door, he said. A backup officer arrived after the shooting.
